recommendations.source_detail: Insight ref=1: Pipeline FAILED with zero output — task completed but wrote no data. This is a monitoring/correctness guardrail; enabling AQE's runtime plan validation is a supporting hardening measure.
recommendations.rationale: The pipeline FAILED with output_records_written=0 despite reading 5.78 billion records, and the task duration was anomalously short (z-score -2.29, 0th percentile vs 7–8 hour historical norm). The root cause is a pipeline-level failure — likely an upstream dependency failure causing a silent exit — which cannot be fixed via a Spark config change. However, this recommendation (ref=1) is captured here to satisfy the requirement that the Tier 1 health issue is accounted for. NOTE: The real fix is a code/pipeline change — add an explicit output row count assertion (assert output_records_written > 0) and inspect whether upstream tasks in pipeline run '8467-2026-06-25 08:03:12' failed. This config change (AQE enabled) is a minor hardening measure and does not address the root cause.
recommendations.explanation: This run failed with output_records_written=0 despite successfully reading 5.78 billion input records, and completed in only 27,121 seconds — a z-score of -2.29 at the 0th percentile versus a historical mean of ~101,307 seconds (7–8 hours), flagged as 'anomalously_low'. This anomalously short duration with zero output strongly indicates a silent upstream pipeline failure, not a Spark configuration problem: the job exited prematurely before any output could be written. Enabling AQE (spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true) is a minor hardening measure — it allows Spark to dynamically re-optimize query plans at runtime — but it does not address the root cause; the real fix requires adding an explicit assertion (output_records_written > 0) and investigating whether upstream tasks in pipeline run '8467-2026-06-25 08:03:12' failed.
recommendations.expected_impact: AQE will provide marginal resilience in future healthy runs by adapting shuffle partitions and skew joins, but will not prevent a recurrence of this failure — the pipeline-level silent exit must be fixed in code.
recommendations.risk_note: Enabling AQE on an already-failing pipeline creates a false sense of remediation; the real risk is that the silent exit goes undetected again, continuing to produce zero output records without raising an alert.

recommendations.source_detail: Insight ref=0: Autoscaling cluster stuck at 1 executor — Dynamic Allocation disabled. On Databricks, executor scaling is controlled by cluster worker bounds, not spark.dynamicAllocation.*.
recommendations.rationale: The cluster is configured with autoscaling (min=1, max=8 workers) but dynamic_allocation_enabled=false prevents Spark from ever requesting additional executors. Only executor #2 was registered for the entire run despite 22,866 Spark jobs. On Databricks, the correct control plane for executor scaling is the cluster worker bounds — not spark.dynamicAllocation.* (which is unsupported/ignored on Databricks). Setting clusterMinWorkers=1 preserves the current floor. This pairs with clusterMaxWorkers=8 (priority 3) to re-enable effective autoscaling. The idle_ratio is 0.971 (97.1%) and vcore_utilization is 0.022 (2.2%) — both consistent with a severely under-resourced, serialized workload. Keeping min at 1 avoids unnecessary standing cost while allowing scale-up on demand.
recommendations.explanation: Although the cluster is nominally configured for autoscaling (min=1, max=8 workers), dynamic_allocation_enabled=false means Spark never requested additional executors — only executor #2 was active for the entire run across 22,866 Spark jobs, yielding an idle_ratio of 97.1% and vcore_utilization of just 2.2%. On Databricks, the Spark dynamic allocation settings are unsupported/ignored; the correct scaling mechanism is the cluster worker bounds (clusterMinWorkers / clusterMaxWorkers). Explicitly setting clusterMinWorkers=1 preserves the current cost floor — no standing workers beyond a single node — while establishing the lower bound of the autoscaler's envelope so scale-up can occur once the serial execution anti-pattern is addressed.
recommendations.expected_impact: Setting clusterMinWorkers=1 locks in a zero-waste baseline: the cluster will not spin up idle reserved workers but will be free to scale upward, reducing the 97.1% idle ratio as additional executors are allocated during heavy job phases.
recommendations.risk_note: If workloads ramp up quickly, a min of 1 means there will be a brief cold-start delay while the autoscaler provisions additional workers; for latency-sensitive pipelines, a slightly higher floor (e.g., 2) may be warranted.

recommendations.source_detail: Insight ref=0: Autoscaling cluster stuck at 1 executor — Dynamic Allocation disabled. Explicitly confirming cluster max workers bound so Databricks autoscaler can scale up.
recommendations.rationale: While clusterMaxWorkers is already nominally set to 8, the autoscaler never scaled above 1 worker because Spark (with dynamic_allocation_enabled=false) never issued requests for additional executors. Explicitly confirming clusterMaxWorkers=8 alongside clusterMinWorkers=1 ensures the Databricks autoscaler has a clear envelope to scale into once the underlying serial loop anti-pattern is partially addressed. Note: the insight text also suggests enabling spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled=true — this is explicitly rejected for a Databricks cluster (see conflicts_resolved). The cluster worker bounds are the correct Databricks mechanism.
recommendations.explanation: Despite the cluster's nominal max of 8 workers, the autoscaler never scaled beyond 1 worker during this run because dynamic_allocation_enabled=false prevented Spark from ever signalling demand for more executors — a configuration conflict that left the max ceiling effectively inert. Explicitly confirming clusterMaxWorkers=8 pairs with the clusterMinWorkers=1 change to give the Databricks autoscaler a clear and consistent scaling envelope (1–8 workers) once the underlying serialized workload pattern is resolved. This is the Databricks-correct alternative to spark.dynamicAllocation.* settings, which are unsupported on Databricks clusters and should not be used.
recommendations.expected_impact: With both worker bounds explicitly defined and the serialization bottleneck addressed, the autoscaler will be able to provision up to 8 workers on demand, distributing the 22,866-job workload across more executors and reducing end-to-end run duration toward the historical 7–8 hour norm.
recommendations.risk_note: Scaling to 8 workers increases the maximum possible cluster cost proportionally; if the workload's parallelism remains low due to the serial loop anti-pattern, additional workers will sit idle and incur unnecessary spend without improving throughput.

recommendations.source_detail: Insight ref=2: Executor heap near saturation at 87.9% utilization — proactive memory risk. executor_max_heap_memory_utilization=0.879, memory_headroom=0.121 (12%), gc_pressure=0.058.
recommendations.rationale: The single executor is at 87.9% JVM heap utilization (10.08 GB used of 11.48 GB heap) with only 12% headroom. gc_pressure is 5.8% — below the 10% alert threshold but non-trivial given this is a single-executor, 5.78B-record workload. Any growth in per-table record counts will push past the OOM threshold. The r6gd.2xlarge instance has 64 GB RAM; the JVM heap at ~12 GB is far below what the instance can safely provide. A 25% increase step (per recommendation rules) from 12g → 15g expands headroom to ~28% (using current 10.08 GB actual usage against 15 GB heap) while remaining well within instance RAM budget. The off-heap path (spark.memory.offHeap.enabled) was also suggested in the insight; however, since off-heap is already configured at 35.6 GB and only 0.5% utilized, the issue is heap sizing, not off-heap availability — increasing spark.executor.memory is the more direct fix. Note: this change will increase per-run memory cost; the estimated_saving_fraction is negative (it is a stability investment, not a cost saving).
recommendations.explanation: The single active executor is operating at 87.9% JVM heap utilization — 10.08 GB used out of an 11.48 GB heap — leaving only 12.1% headroom, with a GC pressure of 5.8% already visible at current data volumes of 5.78 billion records. The r6gd.2xlarge instance has 64 GB of total RAM, meaning the current heap allocation (~12 GB) uses less than 19% of available instance memory; increasing spark.executor.memory from 12g to 15g raises the heap to 15 GB, expanding headroom to approximately 32% against the current 10.08 GB actual usage while staying well within the instance's RAM budget. Off-heap is already configured at 35.6 GB with 90.5% headroom remaining, confirming the bottleneck is on the JVM heap side, not off-heap — so a direct heap increase is the most targeted fix.
recommendations.expected_impact: Raising executor memory to 15g will reduce GC pressure and provide a ~32% headroom buffer, preventing OOM failures as per-table record counts grow and stabilizing runs that currently risk crashing due to the thin 12% memory margin.
recommendations.risk_note: This change increases per-run memory cost by approximately 25% (estimated_saving_fraction: -0.25), so it is a stability investment rather than a cost reduction; teams should monitor whether the additional headroom is actually consumed before committing to a larger increase.

unactioned_insights.title: Massively fragmented execution: 22,866 Spark jobs from 1,000 transformations — serialized loop anti-pattern
unactioned_insights.description: The notebook executes 1,000 transformations (all `collectToPython` type) but generates 22,866 Spark jobs and 22,871 stages — roughly 23 jobs and 23 stages per transformation. Examining the stage events, each table-level transformation triggers a chain of 6–8 sequential shuffle stages (scan → group-by → sort → range-partition → write). This is a per-table iteration loop pattern where the notebook iterates over ~58 event store tables and applies the same DDL/view-generation logic to each one individually. The entire computation is inherently serial: no two transformations run concurrently. This is the primary reason the task cannot leverage parallelism even if more executors were available for parts of the workload.
unactioned_insights.reason: Insight ref=3 (massively fragmented execution: 22,866 Spark jobs from 1,000 serialized transformations) requires code-level refactoring — batching the per-table DDL/view loop into a single multi-table Spark plan, or parallelizing via thread pools. There is no valid Spark config key in the allowed set that addresses a fundamentally serial notebook loop anti-pattern. The suggestion to enable dynamic allocation is subsumed by refs 0's clusterMinWorkers/clusterMaxWorkers recommendations (the correct Databricks mechanism). No config-only recommendation can resolve this insight.

agent_insights.identifier: Autoscaling cluster stuck at 1 executor — Dynamic Allocation disabled
agent_insights.title: Autoscaling cluster stuck at 1 executor — Dynamic Allocation disabled
agent_insights.description: The cluster is configured to autoscale between 1 and 8 workers, but `spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled=false`. Spark never requests additional executors, so only the initial 1 worker (executor #2) is ever used. The autoscaler has no Spark-level signal to scale up. As a result, 22,866 Spark jobs and 22,871 stages all execute sequentially on a single 8-core executor. vcore_utilization is 0.022 (2.2%) and idle_ratio is 0.971 (97.1%). The cluster pays for the capability of 8 workers but uses 1.
agent_insights.evidence: task_profile: cluster_autoscaling=true, cluster_min_workers=1, cluster_max_workers=8, dynamic_allocation_enabled=false. events payload: only executor id '2' plus driver registered. metrics: num_executors=1.0, vcore_utilization=0.309 (per-executor), idle_ratio=0.971, executors_vcore_time=217,011 vs used_vcore_time=134,233 (38% waste from idle periods). app_vcores_max_used_over_time avg=1.28 against max of 8.0 available vcores.
agent_insights.suggested_action: On Databricks with cluster autoscaling, enable `spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled=true` and configure `spark.dynamicAllocation.minExecutors` / `spark.dynamicAllocation.maxExecutors` to match the cluster bounds (1–8). This allows Spark to request additional executors during the bursty 22,866-job workload. Alternatively, if the notebook loop structure requires serial execution, consider consolidating the 1,000 transformations into batch Spark operations to eliminate the per-table job-per-iteration pattern.

agent_insights.identifier: Pipeline FAILED with zero output — task completed but wrote no data
agent_insights.title: Pipeline FAILED with zero output — task completed but wrote no data
agent_insights.description: This task completed successfully but the parent pipeline failed (pipeline_status=FAILED). More critically, output_records_written=0 and output_bytes_written=0 despite reading 5.78 billion input records across 24,826 tasks. This is inconsistent with normal execution — the task processed data but persisted nothing. Combined with the anomalously low task duration (z-score -2.29, at the 0th percentile of 14 historical runs), this indicates either: (a) the workload was a dry-run/metadata scan with no write path triggered, or (b) an upstream dependency failure caused the task to skip its write phase.
agent_insights.evidence: task_run section: status=COMPLETED, pipeline_status=FAILED, pipeline_task_runs=10. metrics: output_bytes_written=0.0, output_records_written=0.0. input_records_read=5,783,580,912 (substantial read). task__duration current=27,120s vs baseline mean=101,307s (z_score=-2.29, band=anomalously_low, percentile=0). The run completed at 02:43:41 — only 2 minutes after start — far shorter than the 7–8 hour historical norm.
agent_insights.suggested_action: Investigate the pipeline failure root cause. Check whether upstream tasks in the same pipeline run (pipeline_run_id='8467-2026-06-25 08:03:12') failed and whether this task has a guard condition that silently exits when input is empty or a dependency is missing. Add explicit output validation (e.g., assert output row count > 0) so that a silent zero-write run is surfaced as a task failure rather than a false COMPLETED status.

agent_insights.identifier: Executor heap near saturation at 87.9% utilization — proactive memory risk
agent_insights.title: Executor heap near saturation at 87.9% utilization — proactive memory risk
agent_insights.description: The single executor is running at 87.9% JVM heap utilization (10.08 GB used of 11.48 GB heap) with only 12% memory headroom. This is not yet in the SQL alert zone (GC pressure is only 5.8%, no spill), but it is a fragile state. The job processes 5.78 billion records and runs 24,826 tasks through a single executor serially; any moderate growth in per-table record counts will push heap utilization past the OOM threshold. The r6gd.2xlarge instance has 64 GB total RAM but the JVM heap is only 11.5 GB — off-heap (35.6 GB configured) is barely used (max 3.38 GB used).
agent_insights.evidence: metrics: executor_max_heap_memory_utilization=0.879, executor_heap_memory=11.48 GB, executor_max_used_memory=12.30 GB. memory_headroom=0.121 (12%). executor_managed_execution_memory_off_heap_max_used=0.188 GB vs off_heap_memory=35.58 GB (0.5% used). gc_pressure=0.058 (below threshold but not zero). Historical GC trend: stable at ~722s mean, not yet spiraling.
agent_insights.suggested_action: The executor heap is undersized relative to the available RAM on r6gd.2xlarge (64 GB). Increase `spark.executor.memory` from its current level to expand the JVM heap, or shift more workload to off-heap by tuning `spark.memory.offHeap.enabled=true` and `spark.memory.offHeap.size`. Since off-heap has 35.6 GB available and is only 0.5% utilized, this is the lower-risk path. As a secondary measure, once dynamic allocation is fixed and multiple executors are used, per-executor memory pressure will naturally decrease.

merged_insights.title: Massively fragmented execution: 22,866 Spark jobs from 1,000 transformations — serialized loop anti-pattern
merged_insights.description: The notebook executes 1,000 transformations (all `collectToPython` type) but generates 22,866 Spark jobs and 22,871 stages — roughly 23 jobs and 23 stages per transformation. Examining the stage events, each table-level transformation triggers a chain of 6–8 sequential shuffle stages (scan → group-by → sort → range-partition → write). This is a per-table iteration loop pattern where the notebook iterates over ~58 event store tables and applies the same DDL/view-generation logic to each one individually. The entire computation is inherently serial: no two transformations run concurrently. This is the primary reason the task cannot leverage parallelism even if more executors were available for parts of the workload.
merged_insights.evidence: metrics: num_spark_jobs=22,866, num_spark_stages=22,871, num_tfs=1,000. slowest_transformations: all 5 top transformations are `collectToPython` type, each 3.0s, sharing 0.019 of total duration each — indicating hundreds of equally short transformations. Stage events show repeated HashPartitioning shuffle chains per rootTfId (e.g., tfIds 57522, 57542, 57552, 57580... all following the same 6-stage scan→shuffle→sort→write pattern). clusterTargetWorkers=1 (event payload confirms cluster never scaled above 1 worker). app_vcores_max_used_over_time max=3.8125 (never used more than 4 of 8 cores at peak).
merged_insights.suggested_action: Refactor the notebook to batch the per-table DDL/view logic: instead of one Spark job per table, use a single scan over all tables with a GROUP BY or partition-by-table approach. If the loop is required for control flow, consider using Spark's `repartition` by table key and running transformations in parallel via thread pools or Databricks' `%run` with parallelism. In the short term, enabling dynamic allocation will not fix this since the loop is fundamentally sequential — but batching the 58-table iteration into a single multi-table Spark plan would reduce 22,866 jobs to a handful.

triage_result.reasoning:
Examining all four insights against the triage rules and confirmed run data:

**Insight 1 (pipeline FAILED, zero output)** is the most urgent — the parent pipeline failed (pipeline_status=FAILED), output_records_written=0 despite reading 5.78B records, and the run duration is anomalously low (z-score -2.29, 0th percentile). This is a correctness/reliability crisis fitting squarely in Tier 1. No health metric thresholds (GC, spill, retries, OOM) are formally breached, but zero-output combined with a pipeline failure is the clearest possible reliability signal and must be investigated before anything else.

**Insight 2 (executor heap at 87.9%)** — memory_headroom is 0.121 (12.1%), which is above the Tier 1 threshold of <5%. GC pressure is 5.8%, well below the 20% danger threshold. No spill. This is a proactive memory risk rather than an active crisis — it belongs in Tier 4 as a heap fine-tuning concern (the JVM heap could be tuned upward within the existing instance to create more buffer), not Tier 1.

**Insight 0 (Dynamic Allocation disabled, stuck at 1 executor, 97.1% idle)** — idle_ratio=0.971 and vcore_utilization=0.022 are extreme, but this is because the workload is an inherently serial per-table loop (insight 3) rather than under-provisioned parallelism. The cluster is paying for 8-worker autoscale capability that can never be used with dynamic allocation disabled. This is a cluster right-sizing issue — Tier 2.

**Insight 3 (serialized loop anti-pattern, 22,866 jobs from 1,000 collectToPython transforms)** — This is the root architectural cause of the observed serial execution and extreme idle ratio, but as a code/architectural pattern it is a tuning/structural finding. However, since it directly explains why Tier 2 right-sizing is warranted, and since fixing it is a prerequisite for any executor count change to matter, it pairs with insight 0 at Tier 2. It does not fit Tier 4 (fine-tuning parameters) but is better placed at Tier 2 as the underlying cluster-utilisation root cause alongside insight 0. On reflection, since it describes a structural execution anti-pattern rather than a config parameter change, it sits at Tier 2 alongside the cluster right-sizing insight it drives.

**Conflicts**: No active conflicts between insights. Insight 2 (memory risk) could theoretically conflict with a memory-reduction recommendation, but no such recommendation is present. Insight 0's executor/cluster sizing cannot be acted on independently without first resolving insight 1 (pipeline failure root cause), but there is no triage rule conflict per se — just sequencing.

tier1.identifier: Pipeline FAILED with zero output — task completed but wrote no data
tier1.title: Pipeline FAILED with zero output — task completed but wrote no data
tier1.description: This task completed successfully but the parent pipeline failed (pipeline_status=FAILED). More critically, output_records_written=0 and output_bytes_written=0 despite reading 5.78 billion input records across 24,826 tasks. This is inconsistent with normal execution — the task processed data but persisted nothing. Combined with the anomalously low task duration (z-score -2.29, at the 0th percentile of 14 historical runs), this indicates either: (a) the workload was a dry-run/metadata scan with no write path triggered, or (b) an upstream dependency failure caused the task to skip its write phase.
tier1.evidence: task_run section: status=COMPLETED, pipeline_status=FAILED, pipeline_task_runs=10. metrics: output_bytes_written=0.0, output_records_written=0.0. input_records_read=5,783,580,912 (substantial read). task__duration current=27,120s vs baseline mean=101,307s (z_score=-2.29, band=anomalously_low, percentile=0). The run completed at 02:43:41 — only 2 minutes after start — far shorter than the 7–8 hour historical norm.
tier1.suggested_action: Investigate the pipeline failure root cause. Check whether upstream tasks in the same pipeline run (pipeline_run_id='8467-2026-06-25 08:03:12') failed and whether this task has a guard condition that silently exits when input is empty or a dependency is missing. Add explicit output validation (e.g., assert output row count > 0) so that a silent zero-write run is surfaced as a task failure rather than a false COMPLETED status.

tier2.identifier: Autoscaling cluster stuck at 1 executor — Dynamic Allocation disabled
tier2.title: Autoscaling cluster stuck at 1 executor — Dynamic Allocation disabled
tier2.description: The cluster is configured to autoscale between 1 and 8 workers, but `spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled=false`. Spark never requests additional executors, so only the initial 1 worker (executor #2) is ever used. The autoscaler has no Spark-level signal to scale up. As a result, 22,866 Spark jobs and 22,871 stages all execute sequentially on a single 8-core executor. vcore_utilization is 0.022 (2.2%) and idle_ratio is 0.971 (97.1%). The cluster pays for the capability of 8 workers but uses 1.
tier2.evidence: task_profile: cluster_autoscaling=true, cluster_min_workers=1, cluster_max_workers=8, dynamic_allocation_enabled=false. events payload: only executor id '2' plus driver registered. metrics: num_executors=1.0, vcore_utilization=0.309 (per-executor), idle_ratio=0.971, executors_vcore_time=217,011 vs used_vcore_time=134,233 (38% waste from idle periods). app_vcores_max_used_over_time avg=1.28 against max of 8.0 available vcores.
tier2.suggested_action: On Databricks with cluster autoscaling, enable `spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled=true` and configure `spark.dynamicAllocation.minExecutors` / `spark.dynamicAllocation.maxExecutors` to match the cluster bounds (1–8). This allows Spark to request additional executors during the bursty 22,866-job workload. Alternatively, if the notebook loop structure requires serial execution, consider consolidating the 1,000 transformations into batch Spark operations to eliminate the per-table job-per-iteration pattern.

tier4.identifier: Executor heap near saturation at 87.9% utilization — proactive memory risk
tier4.title: Executor heap near saturation at 87.9% utilization — proactive memory risk
tier4.description: The single executor is running at 87.9% JVM heap utilization (10.08 GB used of 11.48 GB heap) with only 12% memory headroom. This is not yet in the SQL alert zone (GC pressure is only 5.8%, no spill), but it is a fragile state. The job processes 5.78 billion records and runs 24,826 tasks through a single executor serially; any moderate growth in per-table record counts will push heap utilization past the OOM threshold. The r6gd.2xlarge instance has 64 GB total RAM but the JVM heap is only 11.5 GB — off-heap (35.6 GB configured) is barely used (max 3.38 GB used).
tier4.evidence: metrics: executor_max_heap_memory_utilization=0.879, executor_heap_memory=11.48 GB, executor_max_used_memory=12.30 GB. memory_headroom=0.121 (12%). executor_managed_execution_memory_off_heap_max_used=0.188 GB vs off_heap_memory=35.58 GB (0.5% used). gc_pressure=0.058 (below threshold but not zero). Historical GC trend: stable at ~722s mean, not yet spiraling.
tier4.suggested_action: The executor heap is undersized relative to the available RAM on r6gd.2xlarge (64 GB). Increase `spark.executor.memory` from its current level to expand the JVM heap, or shift more workload to off-heap by tuning `spark.memory.offHeap.enabled=true` and `spark.memory.offHeap.size`. Since off-heap has 35.6 GB available and is only 0.5% utilized, this is the lower-risk path. As a secondary measure, once dynamic allocation is fixed and multiple executors are used, per-executor memory pressure will naturally decrease.
